stem: Which of the following is the best explanation for why the event in the photograph became a turning point in American history?

options.text: The crash itself destroyed the American economy in a single day, with no other causes.
options.misconception: No single day destroys an economy; the crash was the trigger, and deeper weaknesses did the lasting damage.

options.text: The crash proved that the stock market had been the only weak part of an otherwise healthy economy with strong farms and sound banks.
options.misconception: The economy had many weak spots, from farms to banks; the market was only the most visible one.

options.text: The crash ended the Great Depression immediately by forcing prices back to normal.
options.misconception: The Depression lasted a decade after the crash; it did not end when prices fell.

options.text: The crash exposed deeper weaknesses — overproduction, farm distress, fragile banks, and buying on margin — that turned a market fall into a decade-long depression.

rationales.A: No single day destroys an economy. The crash was the trigger, and deeper weaknesses did the lasting damage.
rationales.B: The economy had many weak spots, from farms to banks. The market was only the most visible one.
rationales.C: The Depression lasted a decade after the crash. It did not end when prices fell.
rationales.D: Historians treat the crash as the trigger rather than the whole cause. Background: the books list several causes together — overproduction, farm distress, a fragile banking system, speculation on margin, and maldistribution of income.
rationales.general:
1. Separate the trigger from the cause. The crash was the spark; the fuel was already there.
2. List the fuel. Farms were in distress, factories overproduced, banks were fragile, and stocks were bought on margin.
3. Follow the chain. A market fall became bank failures, lost jobs, and a decade of depression because the weaknesses were connected.
4. Name the turning point. After 1929 no one could argue that the government should simply stand aside.
Remember: a turning point is rarely one event alone. Look for the weaknesses underneath that made one event change everything.
